title: The Version of Me You Won't Find on LinkedIn
author: Ash Wright
summary: In this personal essay, senior financial-services leader Ash Wright breaks from decades of curated professional biography to disclose a history of bipolar disorder, alcohol dependence, and two suicide attempts in his early twenties. He traces the arc from crisis and repeated hospitalization through a diagnosis of bipolar disorder, nineteen years of sobriety, and the ordinary, unglamorous maintenance that keeps him well today. Wright argues that leadership rhetoric about "bringing your whole self to work" and psychological safety rings hollow when leaders themselves only disclose the parts of their story that fit a tidy corporate biography. He was prompted to write now after encouraging someone close to him to seek help while realizing he had never modeled that same openness publicly. The piece closes around Australia's R U OK? Day, arguing that asking someone if they are okay only matters if they believe the person asking can handle an honest answer. Written for a leadership and professional audience, it functions as an argument about authenticity, disclosure, and psychological safety in organizational life.
points: Wright discloses a nearly three-decade-old history of bipolar disorder, alcohol dependence, and two suicide attempts by age twenty-two, contrasting it with the sanitized "senior leader" biography he has used in professional introductions.

He frames mental health as a continuum (healthy, unsettled, struggling, crisis) rather than binary, and credits sobriety (19 years), medication, specialist support, and early self-monitoring for his current stability.
He argues that corporate "bring your whole self to work" and psychological-safety language rings hollow if leaders only model disclosure of the parts of their story that fit a polished biography.
The essay was prompted by watching someone close to him struggle and realizing he was asking them to be open about something he himself had never disclosed publicly.
He ties the piece to Australia's R U OK? Day, arguing that asking if someone is okay only works if they believe the person asking can handle the truth.
quotes: For years I’ve advocated for bringing your whole self to work. The truth is, I haven’t always brought mine.

Throughout my career, I’ve unintentionally concealed, or at least sanitised, a story about my mental health that began in my early twenties, eventually led to a diagnosis of bipolar disorder and included periods of significant depression.
Leadership profiles and conference introductions talked about my career, the teams I’d led and things I’d achieved. They didn’t mention private hospitals, suicide attempts or alcoholism.
Eventually, I sought help through a well-known anonymous fellowship, and I’ve now been sober for 19 years.
But asking people to bring their whole selves to work rings a little hollow if we’re only comfortable with the parts that fit nicely into the corporate biography.
I realised I was asking them to do something I hadn’t entirely done myself.
Somewhere along the way, people need to believe we can handle the truth when they answer.

I think that experience has shaped me as a leader. It’s made me slower to assume I understand why somebody is behaving a certain way, more conscious that what we see on the surface can tell us very little, and more aware of the connection between how people feel, how they act and what happens next.
